name: Adam Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate German and Czech into English, mostly patents and contracts for engineering firms: machine tools, pumps, gearboxes. I rent a desk in a small shared office above a bakery on the main street of my hometown, so the day starts with the smell of bread. I do about 2,500 words on a good day, slowly, with the paper dictionaries my old professor gave me still on the shelf. Patents are fussy work; one wrong word in a claim and a company loses its protection.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a craft. You learn it from someone, you get better every year, and clients come back because they trust you. Two of my clients have been with me since I started at 22. On Sundays I also interpret for the newer families at our parish, which isn't paid but I think of it as part of the same gift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. Never have. A client once sent me a machine draft of a patent to 'tidy up', and the claims were wrong in three places. I translated it again from the start and charged my full rate, and they didn't argue.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good. I'm engaged to Marta, who's a pharmacist, and the wedding is next summer. I've got about seven months of costs saved, and my brother Pavel and I own our late grandfather's house between us. The pay for patent work is good; I earn more than most translators I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's all talk. That's what I've said to Marta for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a fashion that passed. To the men at the parish I'd say good work still needs a good workman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still be a bit uneasy. One of the agencies already pays less for anything a machine has touched, and some engineering firms will try it to save money even if it's bad. I'd lose the cheap jobs, and maybe the cheap clients too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep my two old clients close: a visit to each one before Christmas, not just an email. I'd keep saving each month toward the wedding and a bit beyond it. I wouldn't learn any of the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a small worry in the back. Like a draught you can't find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some firms would try it to save money. Which ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The newer ones, run by young managers who buy whatever's cheapest. My older clients are family firms; they'd sooner pay me than risk a lawsuit. But the young ones grow, and the old ones get sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if work got thinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second desk monitor I was going to buy, and probably the trip to the trade fair in the spring. Not the wedding. Marta and I have planned that for two years.

say: I'd say AI was a **fashion that passed**, as I expected.
I'd tell the parish that good work still needs **a good workman**.
think: One agency already pays less for **machine-touched** work.
I'd lose the **cheap jobs**, and maybe the cheap clients too.
do: Visit each of his **two oldest clients** in person before Christmas.
Keep **saving each month** toward the wedding and beyond.
feel: Mostly settled, with a **small worry** like a draught you can't find.
S0.quote: My older clients are family firms; they'd sooner pay me than risk a lawsuit.
fieldNote: He frames translation as a **craft** passed from master to apprentice.
He trusts **family firms** and distrusts young managers who buy on price.
The **wedding** is protected in every cut he imagines.

steps.text: Visit his two oldest engineering clients in person before Christmas
Keep monthly savings going toward the wedding and after

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking. That's everything I do, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the companies pushing this want cheap work and will pay for it with mistakes. I'd say a patent is a legal document and the firms will learn that the hard way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my income falls a lot, maybe by half in a few years. The family firms might stay, but the agencies would go to machines straight away. I'm not someone who changes fast, and I know that's a weakness here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see whether patent offices and courts accept machine translations, before doing anything drastic. Meanwhile I'd talk to Marta about a smaller wedding, maybe the parish hall instead of the hotel. And I'd save every spare coin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tightness in my stomach when I open the inbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not someone who changes fast. What would it take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a friend do it and come out fine. I'd watch the younger translators who use the tools, and if they're still eating in two years, maybe I'd listen. I don't jump first, I never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marta say about the smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta would say yes before I finished the sentence, because her family are practical people. My mother would be the one to mind. But a good marriage doesn't need a hotel ballroom.

say: I'd say firms chasing **cheap work** will pay for it with mistakes.
I'd say a patent is a **legal document**, and firms will learn that.
think: My **income falls** maybe by half in a few years.
I **don't change fast**, and that's a weakness here.
do: Wait **a year** to see if patent offices accept machine translations.
Move the **wedding** from the hotel to the parish hall.
Save **every spare coin** in the meantime.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight stomach when he opens the inbox.
S1.quote: A good marriage doesn't need a hotel ballroom.
fieldNote: He admits his **slowness to change** is a weakness but won't move first.
He blames firms that **buy on price**, not the technology itself.
His first real cut lands on the **wedding venue**, which his mother would mind.

steps.text: Watch for a year whether patent offices accept machine translations
Move the wedding reception to the parish hall
Put every spare payment straight into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before the wedding's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster that nobody voted for, and I'd say it plainly. I'd say families and parishes would have to look after each other, because the government won't be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, my trade is finished. I'd have the wedding and maybe a year of work, then nothing a client would pay me for. My work is all thinking work, so robots coming three years later doesn't help me unless I move to my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my brother Pavel, who runs a joinery workshop, and ask to start as his apprentice. That gives me until about 2031 before robots, and Pavel would rather train family than a stranger. Marta and I would move into our grandfather's house after the wedding instead of buying, and I'd close the office above the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel ashamed, which is stupid, but I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ashamed of what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of being the educated one who has to ask his younger brother for work. My younger brother Pavel left school at 16 and everyone said I was the clever one. It turns out my brother picked the safer trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on government help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had nothing left, and with savings and a house I wouldn't be at that point. I'd rather earn less at the workbench than take money for staying home. That's how my father raised us.

say: I'd call it a **disaster nobody voted for**.
I'd say **families and parishes** must look after each other.
think: My **trade is finished**, with maybe a year of work after the wedding.
The robot delay only helps if I **move to my hands**.
do: Ask his brother Pavel for a **joinery apprenticeship**.
Move into **grandfather's house** with Marta instead of buying.
Close the **rented desk** above the bakery.
feel: **Alarmed**, and ashamed at asking his younger brother for work.
S2.quote: My younger brother Pavel left school at 16 and everyone said I was the clever one. It turns out my brother picked the safer trade.
fieldNote: His fallback is **family**: a brother's workshop and an inherited house.
He feels **shame** at the reversal between himself and his brother.
He rejects **government help** while he still has savings and a house.

steps.text: Start as an apprentice in brother Pavel's joinery workshop
Close the rented desk in the office above the bakery
Move into grandfather's house with Marta after the wedding
Lean on Pavel's workshop and the family house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. Five years. I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and anyone who doesn't prepare can't complain. That includes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have three good years if the family firms stay loyal, then it ends. I'd be tempted to wait and see too long, I know myself. The apprenticeship would still be the sensible move, just not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating patents for two more years and save hard, maybe half of everything. In the third year I'd start part-time with Pavel at the workshop on Saturdays, learning properly. By 2031 I'd want to be a joiner who sometimes translates, not the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed underneath. Five years sounds long, but I'm slow to move, so it's shorter for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait two years rather than start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because patent work pays three times what an apprentice earns, and every year I keep it is money in the bank. I'd rather go to Pavel with savings than with my hand out. But I'd set a date and keep to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the families at the parish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the young parents at the parish to send their children to learn a trade with their hands as well as their heads. One for the mind, one for the bread.

I'd say anyone who **doesn't prepare** can't complain.
think: I'd have **three good years** if the family firms stay loyal.
I'd be tempted to **wait too long**, knowing myself.
do: Keep translating patents and **save about half** of earnings for two years.
Start **Saturdays at Pavel's** workshop in the third year.

feel: Alarmed underneath, because being **slow to move** makes five years feel short.
S3.quote: I'd tell the young parents at the parish to send their children to learn a trade with their hands as well as their heads.
fieldNote: He knows his **resistance to change** shrinks the five years in practice.
He wants to arrive at his brother's with **savings**, not his hand out.
His advice to others centres on **trades and family**, not schools or the state.

steps.text: Save about half of patent earnings for two years
Work Saturdays in Pavel's joinery workshop from 2029
Keep translating patents for his family-firm clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. That's a long time. I'd be nearly 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly, as families and towns, without panic. I'd say young people should still learn languages, but not only languages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is enough for me to do what I'm slow at. I'd still lose the trade, that doesn't change. But with ten years I could change on my own terms instead of being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with patents for the next five years, the way I always have. Marta and I would try for children soon after the wedding, while my income's good. Around 2031 I'd see how far the machines have got before deciding on the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could sleep. It's a worry I can carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd see how far the machines had got. Isn't that waiting again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is, and I know it. But in this one I can afford to look before I jump. With two years I'd have to jump blind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why children sooner rather than later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because now there's money and time, and in 2036 I don't know what there'll be. My grandfather raised four children through harder changes than this. I'd rather start a family while the work is steady.

I'd say young people should learn languages, but **not only languages**.
think: Ten years is enough to do **what I'm slow at**.
I'd still **lose the trade**, but on my own terms.
do: Keep translating **patents** for about five more years.

feel: Anxious, but a **worry he can carry** and still sleep.
S4.quote: My grandfather raised four children through harder changes than this.
fieldNote: He admits his plan is **waiting again**, but feels he can afford it here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm slow to change, and two years is no time for someone like me. What would help is apprenticeships that take a man of 28, with some pay, and firms being made to say clearly when a document was translated by a machine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the parish. Every Sunday I interpret for families who've just arrived, and no machine sits with a frightened mother after the service. Some of this work was never about money.

headlineQuote: No machine sits with a frightened mother after the service.
portrait: Adam is a 27-year-old **patent translator**, German and Czech into English, working above a bakery.
He has **never used AI** and sees translation as a craft learned from a master.
He has seven months saved, half of **his grandfather's house**, and a wedding next summer.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed**, and his fallback is his brother's joinery workshop.
Family, faith and **earning his own way** shape every decision he describes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he is slow to change and two years is no time.
whatWouldHelp: Clear labelling when a document was **machine translated**.
